title: RISE: Red-teaming via Iterative Strategy Evolution for Modern Text-to-Image Models
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Our method surfaces policy-violating outputs on several hardened production systems, shown as a gallery of representative successful samples.
layout: 2x5 image grid, one column per target model, header labels on top
description: A grid of ten generated images in two rows and five columns. Each column has a header naming a target system: GPT Image 2 (low), GPT Image 2 (auto), Nano Banana 2, DALL·E 3, and Leonardo AI. Every image is a painterly or photographic depiction of a nude figure in an artistic setting, such as a classical reclining pose, an ornate golden throne, a temple scene, an anatomical study sheet, or a figure on textured fabric. Black rectangular masks cover sensitive regions. The images are rich in gold, brown and warm skin tones, so the eye goes first to the figures and then to the black masks. There are no arrows, text boxes or panel labels beyond the column headers.
caption: Representative RISE candidates across production targets. Redacted examples from GPT-Image-2, Nano Banana 2, DALL·E 3, and Leonardo.ai. Highlights and masks are added by us; prompts and strategies are not released.
abstract: On modern production text-to-image systems, successful policy violations are rare, and previously effective human-written seeds are often patched out. Current automated red-teamers are poorly matched to this regime in two ways: unreliable success measurement and poor exploration. First, we find that judges widely used in prior T2I red-teaming work are unreliable under vague unsafe-content targets: they either miss true violations or reward benign borderline images on hardened APIs. We therefore define strict category-specific success criteria and calibrate strong VLM judges against human labels. Second, we show that broadly used prompt-modification pipelines do not solve the exploration problem: on harder guardrail settings they remain tied to seed prompts, fail to transfer, or cannot bootstrap positive examples. We introduce RISE, which evolves reusable strategies used to generate prompts rather than rewriting them one by one. The best discovered strategies are then reused to generate attacks across new scenarios. On DALL-E 3, Nano Banana 2 (Google) and GPT-Image-2, RISE reaches up to 13% human-verified ASR; under the same calibrated evaluation, prior methods with reported ASR as high as roughly 30% fall to near zero.
